title: Remove the Armor — Part 1: The Playground & The Helmet
synopsis: Dr. Negin Rajaipour opens with the story of arriving in a new country at age nine — a boy she liked ran up to her on the playground, she couldn't understand a word he said, a red rubber ball hit her in the face, and her brain captured that moment as danger. That snapshot became her first piece of armor: the Helmet. She introduces the neuroscience of how childhood experiences wire the brain to scan for worst-case scenarios and why that protection mechanism becomes a cage for adult entrepreneurs.
takeaways: Every entrepreneur is carrying armor built in childhood — it protected you then and holds you back now
The Helmet is the brain's automatic worst-case scanner: it predicts disaster to keep you safe from pain you once felt
The body gets addicted to familiar emotions the same way it gets addicted to substances — change feels like withdrawal
The brain cannot distinguish between a remembered threat and a real one — stress hormones fire identically either way
90–95% of daily thoughts are either negative or identical to the day before
who: Entrepreneurs who overthink, procrastinate, or feel blocked by a fear they can't name
brief: Dr. Negin Rajaipour on the childhood moment that built your armor — and why your brain is still wearing it.

title: Remove the Armor — Part 2: The Spider, The Voice & The Cloak
synopsis: Dr. Rajaipour leads the room through two live exercises: the spider visualization (shrink the threat, cartoon it, put it in the corner) and the inner critic voice reframe (place it on your palm, play it in Mickey Mouse's voice). Both demonstrate that the brain's perspective on a problem is not the problem itself. She then introduces the Cloak — the armor that keeps entrepreneurs playing small, downplaying their expertise, and waiting until they feel ready.
takeaways: Put distance between yourself and the problem — the nervous system shifts from threat to clarity almost instantly
The inner critic voice is an automatic program, not your actual self — change its tone and it loses its power
The Cloak: playing small, downplaying expertise, waiting for permission, hiding rather than showing up
Your body would rather keep you in familiar stress than risk an unfamiliar happiness
The brain works in maps — if worst-case scenario is your map, that is where it will guide you
who: Entrepreneurs who know their value but can't bring themselves to claim it publicly
brief: Dr. Negin Rajaipour on the live brain exercises that prove your biggest problem is smaller than it looks.

title: Remove the Armor — Part 3: The Shield & The Birthday Party
synopsis: Dr. Rajaipour introduces the third piece of armor — the Shield — which keeps entrepreneurs from making the connections that could change their lives. She tells the story of forcing herself to take off the Cloak at a child's birthday party where she knew no one, introducing herself as a speaker before she had ever spoken professionally, and landing her first corporate workshop three days later. The Shield dissolves when you show your body that there is no danger on the other side of a conversation.
takeaways: The Shield: avoiding rooms, conversations, and connections because they feel risky — and missing life-changing opportunities
Introducing yourself as the future version of you before you feel ready is how you make that future familiar to your body
Taking one social risk — even at a kid's birthday party — can cascade into your first real opportunity
Visualization before an event primes the brain as if you have already done it
Once you remove the armor, intuition gets louder — your body starts picking up signals it was too defended to notice before
who: Entrepreneurs who avoid networking, hold back in rooms, or wait for someone to give them permission
brief: Dr. Negin Rajaipour on the Shield that keeps entrepreneurs hidden — and the birthday party that broke hers.

title: Remove the Armor — Part 4: The Private Video & The River of Change
synopsis: In the most vulnerable moment of the Summit, Dr. Rajaipour plays a video she recorded for herself — alone, never meant for anyone's eyes — from the night she quit her Silicon Valley job to become a speaker. In it she says: 'I am going through a collapse of the old me. I knew that if I didn't listen to it, it really would be self-abandonment.' She closes by teaching the visualization exercise that she promised her former self she would one day share on stage.
takeaways: The river of change is real: when your body fights back hardest is when you are halfway there — do not turn around
Change feels like physical pain because the body is being starved of the chemicals it was addicted to
Talking to your future self — and letting them answer — is not a metaphor. It rewires the map
Visualize yourself a month after completing the scary thing, sitting on your bed proud. Play it as a memory — the brain treats it as experience
You promised yourself something. Keeping that promise is the only thing that separates where you are from where you're going
who: Anyone in the middle of a hard change who needs to hear that the pain is the proof they're moving
brief: Dr. Negin Rajaipour plays the private video she recorded alone on the night she quit her safe life — and kept her promise to share it.

who: Business owners who want a stronger brand presence
